Variants.Content: Nightsong City is located in the Dorne Marche southwest of the Stormlands. It is the ancient seat of the Cullen family. The nights, mountain roads and border songs here are not decorations, but habits left by history: the hostility, robbery and revenge on the other side of the Dorne Pass have made the border lords look out, ride horses and quickly gather as a daily routine for a long time. Nightsong is connected to the Reach, the heart of the Stormlands, and the Passage of Dorne, so its lords must both be loyal to others and maintain viable relationships with their neighbors. Peace on the border never means forgetting old grudges, but means no one draws their sword for the time being.

Entry Nightsong Local families also depend on rainforest timber, game, barren farmland, fisheries, and roofs to protect themselves from storms; any time a road, well, or dock fails, the price falls first on them.

Entry Nightsong They also recognize the accents, laws, and credentials of the Stormlands; reputations can travel great distances from taverns, but true distances must still be measured by wheel, oar, or horse's hoof.

Entry Nightsong If you can supply supplies, avoid danger, and find a guide, it is worth marking in your itinerary; if you don't have these three things, no matter how loud your family name is, it won't be able to save the lost.

Those who repair Nightsong City are familiar with the stone walls, wooden beams, iron doors, tombs, and the seams left by generations of repairs. Those who comfort the families of the deceased are familiar with the old history of the Seven Gods, the Storm King, and the thick stone walls that resist the sea breeze. A stronghold was therefore not just a lord's hall, but also a place where weddings and funerals, vows, labor and local memories recurred.

Entry Nightsong They care about rainforest timber, prey, barren farmland, fish catches, and roofs to shelter from storms. They also look at whether seeds are left after harvesting grain, and whether the city gates are open in times of disaster. When people from afar see coats of arms, what they see is whether there will be food to eat tomorrow.
